info.name: E-Commerce API: End-to-End Tests
info.description:
End-to-end (E2E) tests for the e-commerce API.

**What "end-to-end" means here:** these requests go to the REAL running server (`npm run dev` or `npm start`), which talks to the REAL `ecommerce` database, the same way a browser or the Postman app would. That's different from the unit/integration tests in `tests/*.test.js` (run with `npm test`), which load the app directly in Node and use the separate `ecommerce_test` database.

**How to run:** start the server, then from the `back-end` folder run `npm run test:e2e`. Newman (Postman's command-line runner) runs every request below, in order, top to bottom. You can also import this file into the Postman app (File → Import) and use its Collection Runner.

**Order matters:** the requests form one journey. Register a customer → log in → use the account → delete it. Later requests rely on the session cookie saved by the login request, so run the whole collection, not single requests.

**Cookies:** Newman (like Postman) keeps a cookie jar for the whole run, so after logging in every request automatically sends the session cookie. Requests that must be made logged-out switch cookies off for themselves (see each request's Settings → "Disable cookie jar", stored as `protocolProfileBehavior.disableCookies`).

**Clean-up:** the journey ends by deleting the test customer, so a successful run leaves the database exactly as it was. Each run uses a unique email (`e2e.<timestamp>@example.invalid`; `.invalid` is a domain reserved for testing that can never be a real address), so if a run ever stops halfway, the leftover customer can't block the next run.

**Variables** (collection variables, see the Variables tab):
- `baseUrl`: where the server is running. Override with `--env-var baseUrl=...`.
- `testEmail`, `testPassword`: the test customer's login details (`testEmail` is set fresh by the first request).
- `customerId`: the test customer's id, saved after registration.

exec: // COLLECTION-LEVEL TEST: runs after EVERY request in this collection,
// in addition to that request's own tests.
// Security check: no response may ever contain a password or its hash.
// pm.response.text() is the raw response body as a string (empty for a 204).
pm.test('response never contains a password or password_hash', function () {
const body = pm.response.text();
// pm.expect(...) is Postman's assertion library (Chai). .to.not.include
// fails the test if the text contains the given string anywhere.
pm.expect(body).to.not.include('password_hash');
// Look for the quoted JSON key "password", so error messages that merely
// mention the word (e.g. 'email and password are required') don't count.
pm.expect(body).to.not.include('"password"');

item.name: 1. Register and log in
item.description: Creates a brand-new test customer and logs in as them. The login response sets the session cookie that the rest of the journey relies on.

exec: // PRE-REQUEST SCRIPT: runs just BEFORE this request is sent.
// Give this run its own unique email, so it can never clash with a
// customer left behind by an earlier run that stopped halfway.
// Date.now() is the number of milliseconds since 1970, different every run.
// .invalid is a domain reserved for testing: it can never be a real address.
const email = `e2e.${Date.now()}@example.invalid`;
// Collection variables can be used in any request as {{name}}.
// The request body below uses {{testEmail}}, so set it here first.
pm.collectionVariables.set('testEmail', email);
// TEST SCRIPT: runs just AFTER the response arrives.
// Each pm.test(name, fn) is one named check; if anything inside fn
// throws (e.g. a failed pm.expect), that check fails.
// 201 Created means the account was made.
pm.test('status is 201 Created', function () {
pm.response.to.have.status(201);
pm.test('returns the new customer with a numeric id and the normalised email', function () {
// pm.response.json() parses the body from JSON into a JavaScript object.
// It's called INSIDE pm.test so that if there's no valid JSON (e.g. the
// server is down), this check fails cleanly instead of the whole script
// crashing.
const customer = pm.response.json();
// The id is chosen by the database, so just check its type.
pm.expect(customer.id).to.be.a('number');
pm.expect(customer.first_name).to.equal('E2E');
pm.expect(customer.last_name).to.equal('Test');
pm.expect(customer.email).to.equal(pm.collectionVariables.get('testEmail'));
// Save the id so later requests can check they get the SAME customer back.
pm.collectionVariables.set('customerId', customer.id);

header.description: Tells Express the body is JSON, so express.json() parses it into req.body.

pm.test('returns the customer who just registered', function () {

request.description: POST /auth/login: logs in as the test customer. Newman stores the session cookie from this response and sends it with every following request (unless that request disables cookies).

item.name: 2. Account
item.description: Views and updates the logged-in customer's own account (GET and PUT /account), and checks the API refuses bad input and logged-out requests.

exec: pm.test('status is 200 OK', function () {
pm.response.to.have.status(200);
// Check the exact shape of the response: these five fields and no others.
// .to.have.all.keys() fails if any key is missing OR if there are extra keys.
pm.test('returns exactly id, first_name, last_name, email and phone', function () {
pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.have.all.keys('id', 'first_name', 'last_name', 'email', 'phone');
pm.test("returns the logged-in customer's details, with no phone yet", function () {
const account = pm.response.json();
pm.expect(account.id).to.equal(Number(pm.collectionVariables.get('customerId')));
pm.expect(account.email).to.equal(pm.collectionVariables.get('testEmail'));
// The customer registered without a phone, so it's null.
pm.expect(account.phone).to.be.null;
